title: ASIC warns super funds on service failures
full_text:
The corporate watchdog is threatening to sue superannuation funds for repeatedly ignoring complaints after its sector-wide review revealed shocking failures to properly monitor and handle customer problems and identify systemic issues.
ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said the regulator opened inquiries after it trawled through super fund member complaints from the past two years and identified serious and systemic shortfalls.
Constant took aim at the funds' failure to listen to customers, particularly when different clients flagged the same systemic issues.
"[These are] part of the member services that need to be delivered, and such a fundamental part of understanding what is going wrong or break points in what are increasingly critical services for Australians," she said of the complaints.
Constant said ASIC would take super fund trustees to court and direct them to claw back executive bonuses if there was no improvement in the behaviour, which included funds dismissing complaints as customer errors in more than half of all cases.
The comments come as ASIC prepares to release on Monday a first-of-its-kind analysis of two years of complaints statistics from the independent ombudsman, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA).
ASIC's analysis included 250,000 complaints lodged in the year to June 2025, a 20 per cent increase on the year before. It said about a quarter of the 45 funds considered did not analyse complaints frequently enough to identify systemic issues. Half of these funds identified fewer than five systemic issues in their organisation, and AFCA identified systemic issues at almost twice the rate of the trustees.
Aware Super - Australia's third-largest super fund - identified only a single systemic issue over the period. Asked if this was a realistic reflection of the fund's systems, Constant said that was a question for Aware Super.
She said it was troubling that, in a more detailed analysis of 10 major funds, they attributed the cause of complaints to customer error, awareness or expectations 60 per cent of the time.
In one case study, ASIC found a fund left 250,000 members unable to access documents such as online annual statements for years, despite receiving routine complaints, before investigating and fixing the issue only when one of its staff - also a member - experienced the same problem.
Another fund became aware in 2024 that it had not paid 500 members their entitled retirement bonuses for the past six years. The unpaid benefits totalled $1.3 million; yet, as of May 2026, ASIC said the fund "still had not completed its analysis to confirm all impacted members had been identified and how much each one was owed".
"This is a sign of an immature complaints culture, an immature customer culture, and potentially a concerning sign about risk culture," said Constant.
She warned that super funds would sleepwalk into another member services crisis - such as the high-profile death benefits crisis that rocked big funds like Cbus and AustralianSuper - if standards did not improve.
ASIC's findings reinforce earlier research from Super Consumers Australia that said the sector was failing on basic customer service standards, after a survey of fund call centres found long wait times and a lack of empathy.
Association of Super Funds of Australia chief executive Mary Delahunty said the report highlighted "clear areas for improvement. ASFA will work with super funds to come together to find consistent approaches to analysing complaints and acting on systemic themes in complaint data."
Financial Services Council boss Blake Briggs, who represents retail for-profit funds, said it was "important to identify and address systemic issues before they cause wider harm".
"The government almost two years ago announced its intention to introduce mandatory service standards across the industry in response to unacceptable failures in how major funds had handled Australians' death benefit and group life claims," he said.
"The FSC encourages the government to make this reform a priority."
Misha Schubert, chief executive of Super Members Council, which represents industry funds, said the findings "reinforce the importance of digging into complaints data to inform continuous improvement".
Nine Entertainment Co.
